title: Trump Officials Now Restricting All Legal Immigration Categories
excerpt: From H-1B fees to green card processing, birthright citizenship to refugee admissions, every pathway into the United States faces new barriers under the second Trump administration.
body:
• A USCIS memo issued May 22, 2026 reframes adjustment of status — the process H-1B workers use to get green cards without leaving the U.S. — as an "extraordinary" benefit, potentially forcing applicants to return to their home countries.
  • A $100,000 fee on H-1B visas, immigrant visa pauses for 75 countries, the suspension of the green card lottery, and near-elimination of refugee admissions have collectively narrowed every legal entry route.
  • The Supreme Court struck down Trump's birthright citizenship order on June 30, 2026, but the president signed two new executive orders targeting "birth tourism" on August 6.
  • Indian nationals, who face the longest green card backlogs in the employment-based system, are among the most affected by these cumulative restrictions.

The Trump administration has moved to restrict virtually every category of legal immigration to the United States, creating a web of policy changes that collectively represents the most sweeping overhaul of the legal immigration system in decades. The restrictions span work visas, family reunification, refugee resettlement, birthright citizenship, and the green card process itself.

Green Cards Reclassified as 'Extraordinary' Relief

On May 22, 2026, USCIS issued a policy memo declaring that adjustment of status — the process allowing immigrants already in the U.S. on temporary visas to apply for permanent residency — would be granted "only in extraordinary circumstances." The agency instructed officers to treat it as "a matter of discretion and administrative grace" rather than the routine pathway it has been for decades.

https://x.com/loganclarkhall/status/2089404595646648790

More than half of new green card holders each year have historically been approved through adjustment of status. The policy could force H-1B workers, international students, and family-based applicants to leave the country and apply through consular offices abroad — a process that can take years, especially for Indian nationals who already face employment-based green card backlogs stretching beyond a decade.

"You don't create a roadway, and expand it and expand it, and then suddenly turn it into a one lane highway with an off-ramp to nowhere."

— Angelo Paparelli, Partner, Vialto Law

Immigration attorneys expect legal challenges. The guidance contradicts Congress's 1990 reauthorization of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which explicitly allowed H-1B and L-1 visa holders to pursue permanent residency without affecting their temporary status.

The $100,000 H-1B Fee

In September 2025, Trump signed a proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa holders. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups have filed lawsuits challenging the fee, with DHS fighting cases in multiple courts. USCIS has since issued guidance clarifying that employers — not employees — bear responsibility for the fee, but the policy has sent a chilling signal through the tech industry, where Indian nationals account for roughly 75% of H-1B approvals.

Visa Pauses, Lottery Suspension, and Refugee Cuts

In January 2026, the State Department paused immigrant visa processing for 75 countries. The green card diversity lottery has been suspended. Refugee admissions have been slashed to a record low of 7,500 for fiscal year 2026, down from 125,000 under Biden, with the administration prioritizing white South Africans — of the 4,499 refugees admitted through the program between October 2025 and April 2026, only three were not white South Africans.

Family reunification parole processes were terminated effective December 15, 2025. The Supreme Court in June 2026 allowed the administration to end Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians, with the ruling likely to pave the way for TPS termination for other countries.

Birthright Citizenship: Round Two

The Supreme Court struck down Trump's original birthright citizenship executive order on June 30, 2026, in a 6-3 decision authored by Chief Justice John Roberts. "Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community," Roberts wrote. "We keep that promise today."

Five weeks later, on August 6, Trump signed two new executive orders targeting "birth tourism" and seeking to expand exceptions to automatic birthright citizenship. The ACLU filed a request to block enforcement on August 11. Legal experts have called the new orders "clearly unconstitutional."

"This order seems like a desperate measure by a president who is having a hard time accepting that he just suffered a significant loss at the Supreme Court."

— Rachel Rosenbloom, Immigration Law Professor, Northeastern University

What It Means for Indian Americans

Indian nationals are the single largest group affected by employment-based immigration backlogs, with wait times for EB-2 and EB-3 green cards stretching beyond 10 years. The adjustment of status policy compounds this burden by potentially requiring applicants to leave jobs, uproot families, and process applications from abroad.

The cumulative effect of these restrictions — the H-1B fee, the green card reclassification, the visa pauses — has created what immigration attorneys describe as a system where legal immigration is technically permitted but practically discouraged at every turn.

"Don't overreact. The laws haven't changed," said Louis Massard, a partner at Corporate Immigration Partners. But he acknowledged the memo's biggest practical impact could be discouraging applicants from pursuing legal permanent residency at all.
nri_angle: Indian nationals face the longest employment-based green card backlogs, and the cumulative restrictions on H-1B fees, adjustment of status, and visa processing compound an already decade-long wait.
author: Diaspora Desk
